report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is *plausible but not proven*. Higher chocolate intake has been associated with lower stroke risk in observational research, but this does not establish that eating dark chocolate causes the reduction.

A 2012 prospective-cohort meta-analysis found that people in the highest versus lowest chocolate-intake category had 19% lower stroke risk (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90). A later meta-analysis of 23 prospective studies likewise reported an inverse association with total stroke. These studies support the view, but chocolate type, portion size, diet, exercise, income/health behaviors, and reporting errors can confound such associations.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933736/  
http://heart.bmj.com/cgi/reprint/105/1/49

The biological rationale is cocoa flavanols: trials show improvements in cardiovascular *risk factors* such as blood pressure, rather than demonstrating fewer strokes. The large randomized COSMOS trial tested a standardized 500-mg cocoa-flavanol **supplement**, not dark-chocolate eating; its primary composite cardiovascular outcome was not significantly reduced. Thus it cannot confirm stroke prevention from chocolate.  
https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(22)00275-1/fulltext

Dark chocolate has more cocoa solids and generally less sugar than milk chocolate, but it is still calorie-dense. It should not replace established stroke prevention—controlling blood pressure, not smoking, exercise, and a generally healthy diet. If you enjoy it, choose a small portion of high-cocoa dark chocolate rather than treating it as prevention.  
https://www.heart.org/en/news/2019/02/12/are-there-health-benefits-from-chocolate
